definitions.name: Worst-case and minimax expected regret
definitions.fallback: The minimax value is the infimum over policies of their worst expected regret over the environment class.

definitions.name: Least-explored alternative
definitions.fallback: Among the m alternatives, at least one is pulled no more than the average n divided by m.

definitions.name: Two-environment algebra
definitions.fallback: A quantitative upper bound on the pull-count discrepancy leaves a matching error term in the two-environment regret lower bound.

steps.title: Choose the base instance
steps.detail: Give arm zero mean Delta and every alternative mean zero.

steps.title: Find a lightly sampled alternative
steps.detail: Use the expected pull budget to choose i.succ with expected count at most n/m.

steps.title: Change one source
steps.detail: Raise only that alternative mean to 2 Delta; keep the policy fixed.

steps.title: Write both regret expressions
steps.detail: Expose the base identity and changed-environment lower expression without identifying their expectations.

steps.title: Apply indistinguishability
steps.detail: The compiled Chapter 15 history KL and Chapter 14 Bretagnolle–Huber theorem turn the lightly sampled alternative into a quantitative minimax conclusion.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 13.1 (source statement; proof deferred to Chapter 15)
source_theorem.math: \exists c>0\;\forall k>1\;\forall n\ge k:\quad R_n^*(\mathcal E^k)\ge c\sqrt{kn},
source_theorem.fallback: For unit-variance k-armed Gaussian bandits with means in the unit cube, minimax regret is at least a universal constant times the square root of k times n.
source_theorem.plain: The source states the finite-arm Gaussian minimax order here and explicitly postpones its proof to Chapter 15.

The local expected regret is an ENNReal lower integral on the canonical n-observation history law.

learning_goals: Read relative entropy as an extended-real, direction-sensitive comparison of probability measures.
Distinguish the absolutely-continuous log-likelihood branch from singular support mismatch.
Map a measurable event to Bernoulli probabilities without increasing KL.
Derive the unconditional Bretagnolle–Huber testing bound, including the exp(-infinity)=0 branch.
Keep general coding theory and adaptive bandit-history decomposition outside the compiled §14.2 window.

definitions.name: Entropy and optimal coding
definitions.fallback: Entropy is the expected information content of a discrete outcome and motivates the chapter's coding discussion.

definitions.name: Extended-real relative entropy
definitions.math: D(P\Vert Q)=\int \log\!\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dP,\qquad D(P\Vert Q)=+\infty\text{ if }P\not\ll Q.
definitions.fallback: Relative entropy is the expected log likelihood ratio when P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q, and infinity on support mismatch.

definitions.name: Bernoulli relative entropy
definitions.fallback: The two-point specialization uses zero-mass terms equal to zero and infinity when P assigns positive mass where Q assigns none.

definitions.name: Bretagnolle–Huber testing scale
definitions.fallback: The real-valued scale makes the source convention exponential of negative infinity equals zero explicit.

steps.title: Split the KL branches
steps.detail: Use Mathlib's exact absolute-continuity and log-likelihood integrability characterization; retain infinity on support mismatch.

steps.title: Coarsen to one event
steps.detail: Restrict both measures to A and its complement and prove d(P(A),Q(A)) is at most D(P,Q).

steps.title: Prove the binary bound
steps.detail: Lower-bound binary likelihood affinity by exp(-d/2), then compare squared affinity with the two testing errors.

steps.title: Restore all endpoints
steps.detail: Handle Bernoulli zero/one support cases through the extended-real endpoint convention.

steps.title: Lift to measures
steps.detail: Use antitonicity of the testing scale and Q(A complement)=1-Q(A) to obtain the source theorem in the P-to-Q KL direction.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 14.2 / Eq. (14.7) (Bretagnolle–Huber)
source_theorem.fallback: For two probability measures and any measurable event, the sum of the P error on A and the Q error on its complement is at least one half times exponential negative relative entropy.
source_theorem.plain: Observing an event cannot make two laws easier to distinguish than their full relative entropy permits.
source_theorem.boundary: BanditRLProof.LowerBounds.bretagnolleHuber compiles this unconditional measure/event theorem with D(P,Q), Q(A complement), and an explicit zero scale at infinite KL. It does not claim §14.1 source coding, full Exercise 14.10, or the Chapter 15 adaptive-history chain rule.

definitions.name: Bandit-history divergence
definitions.fallback: The divergence compares finite action/reward histories generated by the same possibly randomized policy in two environments.

definitions.name: Unit-variance Gaussian arm
definitions.fallback: Each arm is a real Gaussian probability law with the requested mean and variance exactly one.

definitions.name: Equal-variance Gaussian KL
definitions.fallback: The relative entropy between unit-variance Gaussians is one half the squared difference of their means.

definitions.name: Source minimax gap
definitions.fallback: The tuned gap makes the information exponent exactly one half and is at most one half when k-1 is at most n.

steps.title: Choose the base instance
steps.detail: Set the first Gaussian mean to Delta and all other means to zero.

steps.title: Find a least-explored alternative
steps.detail: Use the compiled Chapter 13 averaging leaf to choose i>1 with E[T_i(n)] at most n/(k-1).

steps.title: Change one arm
steps.detail: Raise only arm i to mean 2 Delta; its compiled arm-level KL cost is 2 Delta squared.

steps.title: Lift KL to histories
steps.detail: The compiled Lemma 15.1 route recursively applies the same-policy conditional-kernel chain rule and rewrites policy-arm masses as lower integrals of realized pull counts.

steps.title: Test and tune
steps.detail: Apply Chapter 14 Bretagnolle–Huber to the source event T_1(n) at most n/2 (Lean's zero-based Fin 0 / T_0), choose Delta=sqrt((k-1)/(4n)), and use exp(-1/2) at least 16/27 to recover the exact 1/27 terminal.

source_theorem.label: Lemma 15.1 / Eq. (15.1) and Theorem 15.2
source_theorem.fallback: History KL is the first-law expected sum of arm KL costs under one common policy; the Gaussian construction then yields regret at least one twenty-seventh times the square root of (k-1)n.
source_theorem.plain: The theorem converts indistinguishability of one-coordinate Gaussian alternatives into a finite-arm minimax regret obstruction.
source_theorem.boundary: BanditRLProof.LowerBounds.banditHistoryRelativeEntropy_eq_expectedPulls_sum compiles Lemma 15.1 in the source KL direction with first-law realized expected pulls. BanditRLProof.LowerBounds.finiteArmedGaussianMinimaxLowerBound then compiles Theorem 15.2 for every randomized HistoryAlgorithm, k>1, and n at least k-1, returning a unit-cube mean vector and expected pseudo-regret at least sqrt((k-1)n)/27. The local inclusive lastRound contains lastRound+1 observations, so the n-round theorem uses lastRound=n-1.

quantifier_contract: For every measurable, possibly randomized nonanticipating finite-history policy, there exists a unit-variance Gaussian environment.
Every environment mean lies in the unit cube [0,1]^k, with k>1 and n at least k-1.
The result bounds actual ENNReal expected pseudo-regret on the canonical generated history law; it is the standard Lemma 4.5-equivalent regret form used by the source.
Lean's inclusive lastRound contains lastRound+1 observations, so the n-round theorem is instantiated at lastRound=n-1.

definitions.name: Policy consistency (Definition 16.1)
definitions.fallback: One policy is consistent over the class when its regret is smaller than every positive polynomial order on every environment.

definitions.name: Distribution-class information cost
definitions.fallback: The information cost is the least original-to-alternative KL among laws in the class whose mean is strictly above the target mean.

definitions.name: Per-arm asymptotic information constraint
definitions.fallback: A consistent policy must sample each suboptimal arm at a logarithmic rate set by the cheapest confusing alternative.

definitions.name: Finite-time Gaussian lower-bound shape
definitions.fallback: Under the local C times n to the p regret envelope, the Gaussian lower bound sums the positive part of one explicit logarithmic term per suboptimal arm.

steps.title: Freeze consistency
steps.detail: Require R_n(pi,nu)/n^p to converge to zero for every environment in the class and every real p>0.

steps.title: Choose a confusing alternative
steps.detail: Change one suboptimal arm to a law in its component class whose mean is strictly above the original optimal mean and whose original-to-alternative KL approaches d_inf.

steps.title: Lift arm KL to history KL
steps.detail: Use the compiled one-arm specialization of the one-common-policy Lemma 15.1 identity to obtain the original-law realized expected pull-count cost.

steps.title: Charge both event errors
steps.detail: The compiled pathwise and integrated producers charge A to the original changed-arm gap and A-complement to the changed environment's non-changed-arm margin, under the same canonical history laws.

steps.title: Extract the rate
steps.detail: Use the compiled consistency power/log leaves, then take the required liminf and sum gap times expected pulls; the bandit terminal remains blocked.

steps.title: Specialize finite time
steps.detail: For Theorem 16.4 shift a Gaussian mean by Delta_i(1+epsilon), apply Lemma 16.3, and retain the exact positive part and factor 2/(1+epsilon)^2.

learning_goals: Distinguish deterministic expected regret, stochastic random pseudo-regret, and adversarial random regret.
Preserve each probability direction, confidence quantifier, logarithm, square root, and constant in Theorem 17.1 and Corollaries 17.2–17.3.
Understand why Theorem 17.4 first randomizes a bounded reward matrix and then extracts one deterministic matrix with Claim 17.5.
Track the shared Gaussian noise, clipping count, pull-small event, and pathwise regret comparison without inventing independence across arms.

definitions.name: Stochastic random pseudo-regret
definitions.fallback: Random pseudo-regret is the sum of each gap times its random pull count.

definitions.name: Theorem 17.1 threshold
definitions.fallback: One quarter multiplies the minimum of the horizon and the confidence-dependent expected-regret tradeoff.

definitions.name: Corollary 17.2 threshold
definitions.fallback: The minimax stochastic threshold keeps one half inside the square root and one quarter outside the whole minimum.

definitions.name: Theorem 17.4 adversarial threshold
definitions.fallback: The adversarial random-regret obstruction scales as a universal constant times the square root of horizon, arms, and the log confidence penalty.

definitions.name: Claim 17.5 first-moment witness
definitions.fallback: If the average tail probability over random reward matrices is at least delta, at least one deterministic matrix has tail probability at least delta.

definitions.name: Equation (17.8) regret bridge
definitions.fallback: Random regret is at least the gap times the rounds that neither pull the hard arm nor hit a clipping boundary.

steps.title: Stochastic: select the least-pulled alternative arm
steps.detail: Use the uniform expected-regret envelope to control one arm among i>1, then raise only its Gaussian mean by 2Δ.

steps.title: Stochastic: compare the two history laws
steps.detail: Apply Bretagnolle–Huber with the compiled original-to-alternative history KL identity under the same randomized policy; the Chapter 17 tail-event consumer remains open.

steps.title: Stochastic: calibrate Δ and preserve the tail event
steps.detail: Choose the exact minimum in the source and keep the outer quarter, log(1/(4δ)), and probability at least δ.

steps.title: Adversarial: sample a correlated clipped-normal reward matrix
steps.detail: Share one Gaussian noise variable across arms at each round, while keeping each arm IID across time; do not assume within-round independence.

steps.title: Adversarial: combine pull and clipping events
steps.detail: Claim 17.6 supplies probability 2δ, Claim 17.7 removes at most δ, and Eq. (17.8) leaves regret at least nΔ/4.

steps.title: Adversarial: extract a deterministic witness
steps.detail: Apply the compiled Claim 17.5 first-moment theorem to obtain one reward matrix x with the desired random-regret tail.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 17.1 (stochastic high-probability lower bound)
source_theorem.plain: A policy whose expected regret is uniformly at most B times the square root of (k−1)n over the Gaussian class must have, on some instance, random pseudo-regret above the exact confidence threshold with probability at least delta.
source_theorem.fallback: The uniform expected-regret premise forces an exact random-pseudo-regret tail obstruction on some unit-Gaussian instance.
source_theorem.boundary: The threshold definition and Lemma 15.1 same-policy history KL identity compile, but the theorem does not: its stochastic tail-event consumer and constant assembly remain absent. Corollaries 17.2–17.3 and Theorem 17.4 are also blocked and are not implied by the compiled leaves.
